“The Montreal YMCA is a part- 
nership of volunteers and staff 
committed to the fulfilment of 
people in spirit, mind and body, 
and to the development of self- 
reliance in the individual and the 
community. 


Through its actions, programs 
and services, the Montreal YMCA 
will reflect the needs and aspira- 
tions of the community and will 
work with individuals, local com- 
munities and communities in 
developing countries in achieving 
social justice and control of their 
environments.”

1986 was another very successful 
year for the Montreal YMCA. For 
the fourth year in a row, we 
ended with an operating surplus. 
Significant progress was achieved 
in implementing our plans for 
financial development, facilities 
development, marketing, pro- 
gramming, and improving our 
public image. We are particularly 
proud of our work with unem- 
ployed youth, single-parent 
families, young people in conflict 
and minority groups. 


Most of our eight branches en- 
gaged in a thorough strategic 
planning process at the local level 
as a complement to the Montreal 
YMCA’s strategic plan. This has 
resulted in more coherent and ef- 
fective operations. 


Some of the year’s highlights 
were as follows: 


We reached 47% of our $13 
million Capital Campaign goal. 
Over 500 community leaders are 
involved in our fund-raising ef- 
forts. 


The West Island Facility Devel- 
opment Project is well under 
way. We have purchased the 
land, selected the architect and 
approved the design concept. 


The Metropolitan Board of Direc- 
tors approved the Westmount 
Facility Development Project. 


The Montreal YMCA developed a 
partnership with the Argentina 
YMCA. Ten young leaders partici- 
pated in an exchange program. 


The constitution reform project is 
well under way. A broad consul- 
tation process has been set in 
motion. 


Some 101,124 Montrealers 
benefitted from the YMCA’s pro- 
grams and services. Half of these 
participants were adults, and only 
30% of them were registered in 
fitness courses. Fully 45% of all 
participants were enrolled in the 
YMCA’s numerous children’s pro- 
grams, and 8% were registered 
in continuing education classes. 


Much work was done to complete 
our newest operating unit, 
located in the Guy Favreau 
Complex. The new YMCA opened 
its doors in September 1986. 


Bernard W. Matte, 
Chairman of 

the Metropolitain Board; 
Sol Kasimer, 

Director General. 


We thank the many dedicated 

volunteers and staff members for 
their tremendous efforts and con- 
tributions to the Montreal YMCA. 


As we celebrate our 135th year, 
we look to the future with op- 
timism.,

Director General of the 
Montreal YMCA 


The YMCA offers a wide range of 
preschool and after-school pro- 
grams for children of various 
ages. Those under age two, for 
example, are offered in-pool and 
gymnasium exercises designed to 
enhance the overall development 
of their motor functions. Other 
activities are added as the 
children’s skills become increas- 
ingly well-honed. Music, dancing 
and gymnastics are taught, and 
children aged four and five are 
introduced to modern technology 
through science and computer 
courses. In 1986, 300 different 
courses were offered to children 
under the age of six by a total of 
100 YMCA employees and 75 vol- 
unteers. 


As for youngsters between eight 
and twelve years of age, the 
YMCA offers fun activities de- 
signed to develop specific skills 
and interests: motor functions 
and awareness of others, for ex- 
ample, are enhanced through 
group games and other activities. 


During the summer months, the 
YMCA day camps provide amusing 
activities aimed at promoting per- 
sonal fulfilment in a safe environ- 
ment. In 1986, a total of 7,500 
children between six and twelve 
years of age attended the camps. 


Over the past year, a grand total 
of 47,000 children between the 
ages of one and fourteen took 
part in the YMCA’s various child 
development programs. 


The YMCA of Canada’s Job Gener- 
ation Project, designed to help 
young people find work, is coor- 
dinated by the Montreal YMCA. 


During its first 16 months of 
operations, the Montreal Job Gen- 
eration intensive program came to 
the assistance of 99 unemployed 
youths between the ages of 16 
and 25. Participants were provid- 
ed with pre-employment training, 
a job-search technique, a group 
experience, individual attention 
and a post-training follow-up. 


Job Generation opens up new 
horizons for unemployed young 
people. In 1985/1986, 79 of the 
99 participants found work, and 
our statistics show that 60 of 
these young people are still 
employed. Thus, the placement 
rate has so far been 80% , and 
the job-retention rate, 76%. 


In addition to its intensive ser- 
vice, Job Generation also offers 
individualized, educational and 
business counselling. In 
1985/1986, 223 young people 
benefitted from this service. 
Overall, 173 participants received 
individual counselling; 127 were 
referred to various employers and 
78 of the latter 127 have found a 
job. 


In January and February of 1984, 
the Montreal YMCA and the 
Asociacion de Jovenes de la 
Republica Argentina, began plan- 
ning an exchange program. Con- 
tacts were increased, and a train- 
ing program was set up by YMCA 
employees and volunteers in 
order to familiarize the partici- 
pants with the economy, history 
and socio-economic situation of 
the South American nation. Final- 
ly, in November 1985, ten young 
people from the Montreal YMCA 
set off for Argentina! 


Several months later, in January 
1986, ten young Argentinians 
were the guests of the Montreal 
YMCA. Like their Quebec counter- 
parts, they were offered the op- 
portunity to widen their horizons 
through contact with a foreign 
culture. 


The exchange program fit in well 
with the YMCA’s mission, as it 
encouraged young people to 
become active YMCA participants 
by taking part in efforts to 
enhance solidarity between world 
citizens. 


The Montreal Job Generation pro- 
gram offers young people the op- 
portunity, or rather a ‘‘second 
chance,”’ to become employable. 
The project organizers have set 
up a bank of employers willing to 
hire young people. To date, some 
50 companies have invested in 
youth by using this service. 


The success of the program is 
proof of the value of the services 
offered. According to the Mont- 
real Job Generation director, 
Graham Weeks, ‘‘Our number- 
one goal is to help employment- 
disadvantaged young people be- 
come self-sufficient and find 
work... Thus, we hope to main- 
tain our impressive placement 
rate.”’ 


Internationally the YMCA is not 
unlike a big family. Association 
members must strive to know, 
understand, help and love one 
another. The Montreal-Argentina 
exchange helped young people 
discover that they are an integral 
part of a world-wide community. 


The project was made possible by 
the total commitment of the 
YMCAs involved, and by financial 
contributions from the Canadian 
International Development Agency 
(CIDA) and the Secrétariat 4 la 
jeunesse du Québec. 


JOR 


RATION 


As health educators, our role is 
to provide people with factual in- 
formation. It is then up to them 
to decide whether they want to 
change their way of living. 


The Y Worry program (stress 
management) offered this year 
helped a number of people im- 
prove their lifestyles. A group of 
adults ranging in age from 22 to 
68 took part in the ten-week 
course, which focussed on 
alleviating stress, a problem of to- 
day’s society. Participants in the 
specialized program learned to 
recognize the causes of stress and 
to control the problem on a day- 
to-day basis. They completed the 
course satisfied and proud of 
themselves. 


The Y Worry program is only one 
of the new programs set up by 
the YMCA to deal with the prob- 
lems of modern living: the Asso- 
ciation also helps people stop 
smoking (Y Smoke) and control 
their weight (Y Weight), and of- 
fers introductory fitness classes (Y 
Introfit). 


In 1986, the YMCA offered Mont- 
realers a full range of programs 
designed to help them stay in 
shape, including exercise classes 
and aquafitness. Racquet sports 
such as squash, tennis, and rac- 
quetball, along with team sports 
like volleyball and basketball, re- 
mained very popular. Jogging, the 
YMCA Spring Race and the Fun 
Runs helped people stay trim. 
Before registering for any of the 
various fitness programs, people 
are strongly encouraged to 
undergo a thorough evaluation of 
their physical condition. 


TEI GA! AT pra wea 


Forty young Canadians between 
18 and 25 years of age, represent- 
ing 13 YMCAs from across the 
country, belong to the Institute, 
which was set up in November 
1985 by the National Council of 
YMCAs of Canada. 


The Montreal YMCA is an active 
member of the Institute. Thus, 
last year, four young Montrealers 
— Nathalie Brault from the Ho- 
chelaga-Maisonneuve branch, 
Monica McQueen from Notre- 
Dame-de-Grace, and Valérie Carle 
and Suzanne Tessier from the In- 
ternational branch — participated 
in the Institute’s training pro- 
gram. Backed up by Johanne 
Johnson, counsellor, and Bill 
Pigott, senior manager — opera- 
tions, at the Montreal YMCA, 
these young women have benefit- 
ted from a series of truly 
unforgettable experiences. The 


> 


group began by attending an in- 
tensive training session, following 
which they returned to their 
home communities for workshops 
on community development, 
leadership styles, interview 
techniques and communication in 
general. Then, at a seminar in 
Ottawa, they were introduced to 
the Canadian political and educa- 
tional systems and economic and 
religious contexts. They also had 
the pleasure of meeting several 
national leaders. 


At the end of their training the 
group left for overseas, visiting 
Thailand, India, Malaysia and the 
Philippines. The six weeks spent 
in Third World countries en- 
hanced the participants’ 
awareness of the world situation. 
Upon their return to North 
America, they met the am- 
bassadors of the countries visited 


The YMCA Youth Leadership Insti- 
tute is dedicated to the training of 
young leaders who will contribute 
to the economic, social and politi- 
cal quality of life in Canada and 
the world. 


a = 


Valérie Carle, Johanne Johnson, 
Nathalie Brault, Suzanne Tessier 
and Monica McQueen. 


‘Senna mn 


at the United Nations in New 
York, as well as other interna- 
tional leaders. 


Through various experiences 
enhancing self-awareness — as 
well as knowledge on community 
service, group dynamics, the 
social context at the provincial, 
national and international levels 
— the Youth Leadership Institute 
teaches young people to become 
our society’s future leaders. 


The Montreal chapter of the In- 
stitute is a concrete example of 
the Association’s commitment to 
the future of our society.

The Montreal YMCA Foundation 
was created in 1983. Its objec- 
tives are as follows: 


®@ To solicit, by all appropriate 
means, and receive all dona- 
tions, contributions, bequests 
and subscriptions of a 
charitable nature, in kind or 
in cash, for the exclusive ad- 
vantage and use of the Young 
Men’s Christian Association of 
Montreal; 


®@ To these ends, to acquire, re- 
tain, administer, invest and 
reinvest these donations, con- 
tributions, bequests and sub- 
scriptions free of charge, and 
channel these funds, with the 
exception of those needed to 
cover the administration costs 
of the Corporation, exclusive- 
ly to the Young Men’s Chris- 
tian Association of Montreal. 


Last year, the Executive Commit- 
tee of the Foundation set up a 
30-member Board of Directors. 
The Board members represent 
three different sectors: corpora- 
tions and foundations that have 
donated to the YMCA, volunteer 
fund-raisers and the Montreal 
YMCA. The names of the 30 
Board members are as follows:

Following the creation of the 
Board of Directors, the Board 
members set up three committees 
responsible for ensuring the 
sound management of the Cor- 
poration: the Finance Committee, 
the Investment Committee and 
the Needs Analysis Committee. 


The Finance Committee is respon- 
sible for the Corporation’s 
operating budget, the financial 
monitoring of the various fund- 
raising campaigns and the draw- 
ing-up of financial statements. It 
is chaired by the treasurer of the 
Corporation, Mr. Marcel Coté, 
who is assisted by Messrs. Ber- 
nard Dubé, Len Liben and Albert 
Hudon. 


The Investment Committee, which 
is chaired by Mr. Maurice A. 
Massé, who is backed up by 
Messrs. Derek Hannaford, Bruce 
Bishop and William Ridley, is 
responsible for investing sums 
originating from two sources: 
funds raised by the various cam- 
paigns, and money donated to the 
Corporation under the Endow- 
ment and Bequest program or by 
members of the Heritage Club. 


The third body, the Needs 
Analysis Committee, examines re- 
quests for financial assistance sub- 
mitted by the Montreal YMCA. It 
comprises five members: Messrs. 
Frank Peterson, Pierre Riverin, 
Harvey Thomson, John Churchill- 
Smith and Victor M. Drury, who 
is also the Committee chairman. 
All requests for financial 
assistance are first of all studied 
by the Corporation personnel. 
The results of such studies are 
subsequently examined by the 
Committee members, who submit 
their recommendations to the 
Board of Directors for acceptance 
or refusal. 


The Montreal YMCA Capital Devel- 
opment Campaign, which was set 
in motion in April 1985, attained 
its ‘‘crusing speed”’ last year. 
Close to $5,000,000 was raised in 
the form of donations and pled- 
ges between June 1, 1985, and 
May 31, 1986. Thus, the Cam- 
paign has already gathered 
$6,100,000, or 47%, of its five- 
year objective of $13,000,000. I 
wish to underline in particular 
the impressive work of the co- 
chairmen of the Corporations and 
Foundations Campaign, Messrs. 
John Churchill-Smith and Ghislain 
Hawey. 


Thanks to the tireless efforts of 
the volunteer canvassers, the 
Board of Directors of the Found- 
ation was able to make four cash 
donations to the Montreal YMCA 
during the 1985-1986 fiscal year. 
In December 1985, the sum of 
$660,000 was granted to the 
Association to pay for the renova- 
tion work at the Hochelaga-Mai- 
sonneuve branch arena. On 
January 27, 1986, $250,000 was 
transferred to the YMCA to carry 
out repairs and replace outdated 
equipment throughout the net- 
work of branches. In April 1986, 
thanks to a $350,000 grant from 
the Foundation, the Montreal 
YMCA was able to purchase land 
in Pointe-Claire for a new West 
Island facility. Most recently, on 
May 20, 1986, the sum of 
$15,390 was paid to the Associa- 
tion to support its International 
Programs division. 


In closing, I wish to underline 
the efforts of the more than 500 
volunteers working for the 
various fund-raising programs 
organized by the Montreal YMCA 
Foundation. Without their zeal 
and devotion, we would not find 
ourselves today, after only 16 
months of canvassing, in the hap- 
py position of having raised 
almost half of our five-year objec- 
tive. I extend my sincerest thanks 
to one and all. 


eke 
Philip O’Brien 
11 


Upon the conclusion of my third 
year as Director General of the 
Montreal YMCA Foundation, | am 
pleased to provide you with an 
update on the progress made by 
our four major fund-raising pro- 
grams. The Sustaining Member- 
ship program has now been in 
existence for three years, while 
the other programs (Members and 
Participants, Endowment and Be- 
quest, and Corporations and 
Foundations) were set up two 
years ago. 


SUSTAINING MEMBERSHIP 
PROGRAM 


During its first two years of ex- 
istence, the Sustaining Member- 
ship program raised a total of 
$172,412 from 1,300 donors. In 
1985-1986, the program succeed- 
ed in gathering $85,783 from a 
total of 500 persons. This drop in 
receipts is attributable to the fact 
that, last year, the Foundation 
transferred all corporation and 
foundation donors from the pro- 
spect list of the Sustaining 
Membership Campaign to that of 
the Corporations and Foundations 
Campaign (which is part of the 
overall Capital Development Cam- 
paign). 


Mr. Victor M. Drury, chairman of 
the Sustaining Membership pro- 
gram, along with the honorary 
campaign chairpersons, wish to 
thank all donors for their 
generous contributions, which 
have helped make the campaign’s 
third year a success. 


The overall 1984-1990 goal for 
the Sustaining Membership pro- 
gram has been set at $750,000. 
The program is aimed at past and 
present Montreal YMCA committee 
members, staff members and 
former employees, and friends of 
the Association. 


12 


MEMBERS AND 
PARTICIPANTS PROGRAM 


Mr. Claude Lemay chaired the 
1985-1986 Members and Par- 
ticipants Campaign, which raised 
a total of $50,593 from more 
than 1,000 donors. 


The 1985-1990 objective of the 
Members and Participants pro- 
gram has been set at $500,000. 
Over the past two years, we have 
raised $90,293 towards this 
overall goal. All money raised is 
used for building repairs and 
equipment replacement at the 
Montreal YMCA branches and at 
Kamp Kanawana, as provided for 
by the strategic plan for the Mon- 
treal YMCA facilities. 


As of 1986-1987, the Sustaining 
Membership and the Members and 
Participants programs will be 
combined to form a single fund- 
raising program. This change will 
enable the Corporation to reduce 
its organizational expenses and 
maximize the team effort of its 
volunteer canvassers. The new 
campaign, to be called the Sus- 
taining Membership Campaign, 
will be held on a yearly basis 
during the months of November 
and December. 


The Foundation extents its 


sincerest thanks to the hundreds 
of volunteers who contributed to 
the success of the Members and 
Participants program, in particular 
those who helped the West Island 
and Westmount branches reach 
their respective fund-raising goals. 
We also wish to thank all those 
who contributed generously to 
the campaign. 


ENDOWMENT AND 
BEQUEST PROGRAM 


Under the dynamic leadership of 
Chairman Maurice A. Massé, the 
committee responsible for the 
Foundation’s Endowment and Be- 
quest program actively solicits 
donations from long-time friends 
of the Montreal YMCA. The funds 
raised by the committee serve to 
consolidate the financial base of 
the 135-year-old Association. In 
addition to Mr. Massé, the com- 
mittee is made up of Messrs. 
William Ridley, Harvey Corn, 
Michael Gutwillig, Alex Duff, 
Marcel Adams, Frank Peterson, 
Kalman Samuels and Keith Far- 
quharson. 


Richard L. Cooper, 

Chairman, Westmount YMCA 
Capital Campaign; 

Mrs. R. Cooper; 

Victor M. Drury, 

past Chairman; Montreal YMCA, 


Donors may stipulate that their 
bequests to the Montreal YMCA go 
to a specific branch or program, 
or be used for a given field of 
continuing interest (e.g., camper- 
ships, youth programs, leadership 
training, construction of new 
facilities, land purchases, etc.). 
No matter how great or small, 
commemorative donations to the 
Montreal YMCA Endowment Fund 
are always greatly appreciated. Up 
until now, the Endowment and 
Bequest program has received 
donations totalling $27,793, be- 
quests in the amount of 
$404,100, confirmed bequest 
pledges amounting to $337,000 
and ten confirmed bequest 
pledges of unspecified amounts. 
As shown by the above figures, 
the Endowment and Bequest pro- 
gram progressed significantly dur- 
ing the 1985-1986 fiscal year.

in 1986-1987.

$2,000,000 divisional objec- 
tive).

corporations and foundations

bute, and the others will

in 1986-1987.

SPECIAL EVENTS 


The Montreal YMCA Foundation 
held two press conferences last 
year aimed at informing volun- 
teers and the general public about 
the progress made by the Capital 
Development Campaign. In addi- 
tion, on October 16, 1985, the 
organizers of the Sustaining Mem- 
bership program launched their 
1985-1986 fund-raising campaign 
in the presence of approximately 
365 people at the Centaure res- 
taurant, located at the Blue Bon- 
nets race-track. 


As for the Members and Partici- 
pants program, the organizers 
launched their yearly campaign 


on January 27, 1986, on the oc- 
casion of a Pro-Musica concert at 
the Salle Maisonneuve, Place des 
Arts, in the presence of more 
than 200 persons invited by the 
Foundation. 


For the third consecutive year, 
the members of the Heritage Club 
of the Montreal YMCA Foundation 
met at the Mount Stephen Club to 
underline their interest in the 
Association. The Heritage Club is 
made up of men and women who 
believe in the mission and the 
traditional values of the YMCA, 
and who wish to ensure that the 
Association’s heritage is passed on 
to future generations. 


Each member of the Club has 
made provisions for the YMCA in 
planning his or her estate, by 
promising to make a cash dona- 
tion, naming the YMCA as the 
beneficiary of an insurance 
policy, by making an immediate 
contribution to the Association, or 
by setting up a special trust fund. 
As the Club expands, the YMCA 
will acquire an increasingly solid 
financial base, which will enable 
it to continue to play an essential 
role in ensuring the well-being of 
the Montreal community.

The Montreal YMCA Capital Devel- 
opment Campaign, the fifth major 
fund-raising effort undertaken by 
the Association since the start of 
the century, got under way in 
1985. As in the case of the 
earlier drives, the Campaign has 
received a significant level of sup- 
port from the Montreal business 
community.

over five years, from 1985 to 
1990. Messrs. John Churchill-

hard-working co-chairmen of the 
Campaign, join with the honorary
